headline: Seiteki is 静 (sei) plus 的 (-teki).

sources.quote: 静(せい) (sei) + 的(てき) (-teki)

headline: Umeboshi is 梅 (ume, “plum”) plus 干し (hoshi, “drying, dried”), with hoshi voiced to boshi by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 梅 (ume, “plum”) + 干し (hoshi, “drying, dried”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 干す (hosu, “to dry”). The hoshi changes to boshi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Hinata is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus な (na, Old Japanese possessive particle) plus た (ta, “direction, side”).

sources.quote: Compound of 日 (hi, “sun”) + な (na, Old Japanese possessive particle) + た (ta, “direction, side”).
The ta element is found in terms such as あなた (anata, “you”, originally “that side (distant)”), そなた (sonata, “you”, archaic; originally “that side (nearby)”).
Other various nanori readings.

examples.ja: 彼らはひなたでからだをかわかしていた。
examples.en: They dried themselves in the sun.

examples.ja: ひなたに座っているのに、まだ寒気がした。
examples.en: Even though I was sitting in the sun, I still felt chilly.

headline: Asamashii is an adjectivization of the verb 浅む (asamu).

sources.quote: Adjectivization of verb 浅(あさ)む (asamu).

headline: オンライン is from English online.

sources.quote: From English online.

examples.ja: 法律の変更で、電子商取引におけるオンライン販売が脅かされている。
examples.en: Legal changes threaten online sales in digital commerce.

headline: Gozaimasu is a sound change from 御座ります (gozarimasu, “to exist”, polite form).

sources.quote: Sound change from 御(ご)座(ざ)ります (gozarimasu, “to exist”, polite form).

headline: Akudoi is first cited to 1694, and its derivation is unclear: perhaps 灰汁 (aku, “lye”) plus どい (doi), or あ (a) plus 諄い (kudoi).

sources.quote: First cited to 1694.
Ultimate derivation is unclear.
* One reference derives this from prefix あ (a, of uncertain meaning) + 諄い (kudoi, “repetitive, tedious, clunky, long-winded, insistent”).
*: However, there is no apparent fitting prefix, only 亜 (a-, “sub-, -ous, -ite”, most often found in chemistry or biology).

* Described in another source as deriving from 灰汁 (aku, “lye; harshness [as a characteristic of flavor or personality]”) + suffixing element どい (doi). This doi is probably from now-archaic adjective 利し・鋭し・疾し・敏し (toshi), modernized form とい (toi, “sharp, biting; fierce, vicious; fast, quick”).
Considering the senses, this might be a case of separately derived homophones, or a case where separate partially-similar terms influenced the meaning.

headline: Zatsu, “rough”, is from Middle Chinese 雜 (MC dzop).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 雜 (MC dzop).

examples.ja: 彼は仕事が雑だ。
examples.en: He is careless and untidy in his work.

examples.ja: お客が雑な作りのスタンドに座って靴を磨いてもらっている。
examples.en: A customer is having his shoes shined on a slapped-together stand.

headline: Daiben is 代 (dai-, “substitute, in substitution for someone else”) plus 弁 (ben, “speech”).

examples.ja: 彼女は家のない人々の代弁をした。
examples.en: She spoke for the homeless.

headline: Yurumu is 緩い (yurui, “loose”) plus む (mu, “-ize, -en”, verbal suffix).

sources.quote: From 緩(ゆる)い (yurui, “loose”) + む (mu, “-ize, -en”, verbal suffix).

Occasionally pronounced with a medial /b/ as 緩(ゆる)ぶ (yurubu), especially historically. Copmpare similar alternation of /m/ and /b/ seen in 寒い (sabui, samui), 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”).

sources.quote: 感(かん) (kan, “emotion”) + 無量(むりょう) (muryō, “immeasurable”)

sources.quote: 家(いえ) (ie, “house”) + 出(で) (de, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 出(で)る (deru, “to go out, exit”))

examples.en: He ran away from home.

examples.ja: 彼が家出したのは事実だ。

sources.quote: Borrowed from English motel.

headline: Kedamono is literally “thing of hair”: 毛 (ke, “hair”) plus だ (da, genitive marker) plus 物 (mono, “thing”).

sources.quote: Literally "thing of hair". Compound of 毛 (ke, “hair”) + だ (da, genitive marker) + 物 (mono, “thing”). Medial -da- is a very rare genitive marker found in compounds, also seen in 果物 (kudamono, “fruit”).

examples.ja: 原始人はどう猛な獣を見ておびえた。
examples.en: The primitive man was frightened at the sight of a savage beast.

examples.ja: ライオンが獣の王であるのと同様、鷲は鳥の王である。
examples.en: As the lion is king of beasts, so is the eagle king of birds.

meaning: to stop, to abort, to discontinue, to close
headline: Uchikiru is 打ち (uchi, verbal prefix adding euphony or emphasis) plus 切る (kiru, “terminate an action”).

morphemes.meaning: verbal prefix adding euphony or emphasis

sources.quote: From 打ち (uchi, verbal prefix adding euphony or emphasis) + 切る (kiru, “terminate an action”).

examples.ja: この交渉を打ち切りたい。
examples.en: We want to break off this negotiation.

examples.ja: 両国は友好関係を打ち切った。
examples.en: The countries terminated friendly relations.

headline: ニュアンス is listed as borrowed from French nuance or English nuance, and is first cited to a 1909 book by Nagai Kafū.

sources.quote: Listed as borrowed from French nuance or English nuance.

Some Japanese sources do not indicate a source language and only list the etymon form, as nuance, which is the format in these works to indicate an origin from English. Other references explicitly list both French and English as source languages, or just French.
First cited to ふらんす物語 (Furansu Monogatari), a 1909 book by 永井荷風 (Nagai Kafū).

examples.ja: その言葉には微妙なニュアンスがある。
examples.en: This word has a subtle nuance to it.

examples.ja: 彼女の考えと私の考えでは少しニュアンスが違う。
examples.en: There's a slight difference between her thinking and mine.

meaning: to bother, to harass, to molest
headline: Nayamasu is from Old Japanese, first cited in the Man'yōshū of 759, as the causative of 悩む (nayamu, “to be vexed”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Derived as the regular classical causative conjugation of 悩む (nayamu, “to be vexed”).

examples.ja: 彼は疑惑に悩まされた。
examples.en: He was assailed with doubts.

examples.ja: 彼らは重税に悩まされた。
examples.en: They were burdened with heavy taxes.

headline: Shamisen derives from the Okinawan 三線 (sanshin), and was originally called 蛇皮線 (jabisen, literally “snakeskin strings”).

sources.quote: The instrument derives from the Okinawan 三線 (sanshin). Originally called 蛇皮線 (jabisen, literally “snakeskin strings”) in Japanese, so named for the way the Okinawan instrument's soundbox is traditionally covered in snakeskin. The traditional jabisen instrument was imported into the Sakai area of Osaka during the Eiroku era (1558–1570), then later modified by biwa luthiers to have the square-shaped shamisen soundbox of today.

The reading jabisen shifted over time to 蛇味線 (jamisen), replacing the 皮 (bi, “skin, leather”) character with 味 (mi) for phonetic reasons, i.e. as ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Then jamisen changed to shamisen, replacing the 蛇 (ja, “snake”) character with 三 (sha , usually read san, “three”) for semantic reasons. The sha reading for the 三 character is irregular.
The shamisen reading is first cited to a text from 1580.

headline: Setsujitsu is 切 (setsu, “keen”) plus 実 (jitsu, “faithfulness”).

sources.quote: From 切 (setsu, "keen," "acute," "intense") + 実 (jitsu, "faithfulness," "sincerity," "fidelity").

examples.ja: 太っているのが私の切実な問題です。
examples.en: Being fat is a serious problem for me.

sources.quote: 最(さい) (sai-, “most”) + 善(ぜん) (zen, “good”)

examples.ja: 正直は最善の策。

examples.ja: 最善を期待しよう。

headline: Bochi is from the Middle Chinese compound 墓地, literally “grave, tomb + ground, region”, in the kan'on reading.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 墓地 (muᴴ dijᴴ, literally “grave, tomb + ground, region”). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin reading mùdì, Min Nan bōng-tē.

headline: Otsu, “2nd in rank”, is from Middle Chinese 乙 (MC 'it), and its modern slang sense is an aggressive clipping of お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu).

sources.quote: Originally from Middle Chinese 乙 (MC 'it), arising from the proper noun sense. Appears in texts from at least 833 CE.
By extension from the moving tone noun sense. Appears in texts from the late Edo period, in the early 1800s.

Derived as aggressive clipping of お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu, used as a kind of greeting at work, literally “that's honorable exhaustion (from hard work)”). The use of 乙 for the spelling is an example of phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

examples.ja: 甲の薬は乙の毒。
examples.en: One man's medicine is another man's poison.

examples.ja: 甲の損は乙の得。
examples.en: One man's gain is another man's loss.

headline: タイル is borrowed from English tile.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English tile.

examples.ja: 屋根から落ちてきたタイルは粉々に砕けた。
examples.en: The tile that fell from the roof broke into pieces.

sources.quote: Appears to be a compound of 沼 (nu, “swamp”) + 間 (ma, “space, area”).

examples.ja: ここに小さな沼があります。

examples.ja: その沼にはサギがたくさん住んでいる。
examples.en: Lots of herons live in the marsh.

meaning: to escape from, to be exempted
headline: Manugareru is from Old Japanese 免る (manukaru), 目 (ma-, “eye”) plus 抜かる (nukaru, “to mistake”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 免る (manukaru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from 目(ま) (ma-, “eye”) + 抜(ぬ)かる (nukaru, “to mistake”).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
